timing_rule: Latest eligible survey year per source within 3 years; same-year observations require sourced fieldwork dates ending strictly before the ruling. Retain tied variants. This is fieldwork timing, not proof of pre-ruling publication.

cases.name: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen

components.decision: Invalidated New York’s special-need condition for a public-carry license.
components.scope: Protects public carry for ordinary self-defense; does not invalidate all objective licensing requirements.
components.locator: Thomas majority opinion Parts II and IV; footnote 9.
components.survey_fit: The poll addresses this named licensing condition. Its simpler self-protection wording does not measure approval of the historical-tradition test.

observations.wording: Paraphrase: Does New York’s requirement to demonstrate a self-protection need for a concealed-carry license violate the Second Amendment?

response_distribution.label: Requirement does not violate the Second Amendment

observations.denominator: Published two-option percentages; item N=2,133 of 2,158 survey respondents. No reconstruction of omitted answers or new weighting. Rounded publisher estimates, not raw counts.
observations.weight: Published topline; respondent weights not loaded
observations.attribution: Stephen Jessee, Neil Malhotra, and Maya Sen, Supreme Court Public Opinion Project (SCOTUSPoll), 2022 and 2024
observations.wording_note: Question and answer labels paraphrased; consult the linked PDF for exact wording and randomized option order.

cases.interpretation_limit: Direction refers to firearm rights, not liberal ideology. The 52.6% point estimate is a narrow lead, not a significance finding.

cases.name: United States v. Rahimi

components.issue: Temporary disarmament after a judicial threat finding
components.decision: Allowed temporary disarmament following a court finding of a credible physical threat.
components.scope: Facial challenge to the restraining-order statute; the Court’s conclusion is narrower than a ban on everyone described as an abuser.
components.locator: Roberts majority opinion Part II and concluding paragraph.
components.survey_fit: The poll names domestic abusers broadly but omits the judicial finding and temporary duration. Its 74.0% estimate is related context, not exact approval of all statutory conditions.

observations.wording: Paraphrase: Does prohibiting firearm possession by domestic abusers violate their Second Amendment rights?

response_distribution.label: Prohibition does not violate the Second Amendment

observations.denominator: Published two-option percentages; item N=2,218 of 2,218 survey respondents. No reconstruction of omitted answers or new weighting. Rounded publisher estimates, not raw counts.
observations.weight: Published topline; respondent weights not loaded
observations.attribution: Stephen Jessee, Neil Malhotra, and Maya Sen, Supreme Court Public Opinion Project (SCOTUSPoll), 2022 and 2024
observations.wording_note: Question and answer labels paraphrased; consult the linked PDF for exact wording and randomized option order.

cases.interpretation_limit: Do not turn a broad group label in the poll into a conclusion about every restraining order or lifetime disarmament.

limitations: Explicit source-based legal coding is an input, not an automated legal classifier.
Contextual matches do not measure approval of the specific holding.
Mixed and unresolved components retain their labels; no scalar direction is inferred.
No pooling, confidence intervals, causal claims, or prediction.
Published toplines, not independently reweighted microdata; exact question wording is in the source PDF.
These deliberately chosen examples are not a representative sample. Narrow percentage leads are not significance claims.
